lena.name: Dr. Lena Reyes
lena.role: field biologist (a scientist who studies animals in the wild)

case.title: One Parent, Two Gardens
case.hook: Last spring I collected seeds from ONE wild beach sunflower on the dunes. I planted some in our sunny dune garden and some in the shady courtyard behind the lab. Now the plants look so different that a volunteer wrote on the tags: “Mixed up? Different parents?”
case.question: Did the seeds get mixed up, or can one parent plant have offspring this different?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

stills.alt: A wild beach sunflower growing on a sand dune: one yellow flower with a dark center and rough green leaves.
Dried brown flower heads on the parent plant. Each one is full of seeds.
A low, bushy patch of beach sunflowers covered in yellow flowers.
One tall, thin beach sunflower stem with only one yellow flower.

Seeds: Dune sunflower seed heads, Miami Beach, Daniel Di Palma, via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0). Pot A: Dune sunflowers, Sanibel Island, James St. John, via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0). Pot B: Beach sunflower with one tall stem, sonnia hill, via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0). The tags and the gardens are part of the story.

clues.t: Babies resemble their parents in inherited traits like body shape, even when other things (spots, stripes, size) are different for now.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: grow the twins
clues.t: Two seeds from one parent: sun and water changed the height, the spread and the number of flowers, but never the flower color or the leaf shape.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 3: stamp the case
clues.t: Some traits are inherited (a pelican’s beak), some come from the environment (a manatee’s scars), and many are both (how tall an oak grows).

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 4: pass it on?
clues.t: Only inherited traits pass to the next generation. A scar, or being thin after a hard year, stays with the parent.

solve.title: What happened in the two gardens?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: Someone mixed up the seeds. Plants that look this different must have different parents.
options.why: Check Clue 2. In Grow the twins, seeds from ONE parent looked very different in sun and in shade. Different looks don’t prove different parents.

options.t: Same parent. Both plants have the same yellow flowers with dark centers and the same leaf shape: those are inherited. The shady plant grew tall and thin with few flowers because it got less sun: that’s the environment.
options.why: Case cracked! The seeds weren’t mixed up. Inherited traits matched; the garden changed the rest. Now write your case report: it’s the questions below.

options.t: The shady plant changed its traits on purpose to reach the sun, so its seeds will grow tall and thin too.
options.why: Check Clue 4. Traits from the environment stay with that plant. They don’t pass to its seeds. And plants don’t choose their traits.

lineup.title: Find the family
todo: Look at each baby’s body shape, not its colors.
Drag each baby onto its parent, or tap a baby and then a parent.
Find all four families, then answer the question.

why.t: Offspring (babies) inherit traits from their parents. Some babies look different at first, but their inherited traits give them away.

lineup.hint: Drag a baby onto its parent, or tap a baby and then a parent.

babies.name: Spotted kitten
babies.alt: A Florida panther kitten with dark spots and blue eyes.
babies.miss: Look at the face and the round ears. Which parent has the same face shape?

babies.name: Fluffy brown chick
babies.alt: A fluffy, rusty-brown chick with long legs, walking in shallow water.
babies.miss: Look at the long legs and long neck. Which parent has them too?

babies.name: Tiny shelled baby
babies.alt: A tiny tortoise with a yellow and orange patterned shell.
babies.miss: A dome-shaped shell and thick front legs. Which parent has the same shape?

babies.name: Striped babies
babies.alt: A group of baby alligators with bright yellow stripes, resting in the grass.
babies.miss: Ignore the stripes. Look at the snout and the eyes on top of the head.

parents.name: Florida panther
parents.alt: An adult Florida panther with a plain tan coat, sitting in the grass.
parents.same: the face shape, round ears and long tail.
parents.diff: the spots and blue eyes. The spots fade as the kitten grows, and its eyes turn golden brown.

parents.name: Sandhill crane
parents.alt: A tall gray sandhill crane with a red patch on its head, standing by a tree in the water.
parents.same: long legs, a long neck and a long, pointed beak.
parents.diff: the fluffy brown feathers. The chick (called a colt) grows gray feathers and a red cap later.

parents.name: Gopher tortoise
parents.alt: An adult gopher tortoise with a domed brown shell and thick front legs.
parents.same: the domed shell and thick front legs made for digging.
parents.diff: the bright yellow shell. It turns brown and gray as the tortoise gets older.

parents.name: American alligator
parents.alt: An adult alligator’s head with eyes and nostrils on top.
parents.same: the wide snout, the sharp teeth, and eyes and nostrils on top of the head.
parents.diff: the yellow stripes. They fade as the alligator grows.

lineup.q: Look at all four families. Which is true?

opts.t: Babies look exactly like their parents.
opts.miss: The kitten has spots and the chick is brown. Do they look EXACTLY like their parents?

opts.t: Babies inherit their parents’ body shape, but some things, like spots or colors, can be different for now.
Babies pick which traits to copy from their parents.
opts.miss: Babies can’t choose their traits. Where do inherited traits come from?

lineup.win: Four families found! Each baby inherited its parents’ body shape. Spots, stripes and fluffy feathers are traits that change as the baby grows. That’s a clue.

verdict.title: Stamp the case
todo: Open a case and read the facts.
Stamp it INHERITED, ENVIRONMENT or BOTH.
Pick the fact that proves it. Stamp all four.

why.t: INHERITED = from the parents. ENVIRONMENT = from where it lives and what happens to it. BOTH = the parents give the start, and the environment shapes the rest.

stories.name: Pelican beak shape
stories.alt: A young brown pelican with a long, straight beak.
data: Every brown pelican has a long beak with a stretchy pouch underneath.
Chicks hatch with a short beak of the same shape. It grows longer.
Pelicans that catch lots of fish and pelicans that catch few have the same beak shape.
stories.stampMiss: Does the beak shape change with what a pelican eats or where it lives? Read the facts again.

proof.t: Every pelican has the same beak shape, no matter how much it eats.

proof.miss: True, but does that prove where the beak shape came from?

proof.t: Some pelicans are bigger than others.
proof.miss: That’s about size, not beak shape.

stories.why: The beak shape comes from the parents. It’s the same in every pelican, whatever its life is like.

stories.name: A manatee’s scars
stories.alt: A gray manatee underwater with two long white scars on its back.
data: Many Florida manatees have long white scars on their backs.
The scars come from boat propellers (the spinning blades that push a boat).
Manatee calves are born with smooth skin and no scars.
stories.stampMiss: Were the calves born with these scars? Read the facts again.

proof.t: Calves are born with no scars. The scars come from boat injuries.

proof.miss: That’s about color, not the scars.
Swimming slowly is why boats hit them, but what proves the scars aren’t inherited?

stories.why: Scars come from the environment, not the parents. Scientists use each manatee’s scar pattern to tell it apart from others.

stories.name: How tall a live oak grows
stories.alt: A huge live oak tree with wide, spreading branches.
data: A live oak acorn always grows into a live oak, never a palm.
In an open, sunny field, a live oak can grow huge and wide.
The same kind of tree squeezed into a small, shady spot stays much smaller.
stories.stampMiss: One fact is about the parents and two are about the place it grows. What does that tell you?

proof.t: It’s a live oak because of its parents, but sun and space change how big it grows.

proof.miss: True, but which fact shows two causes?
True, but that doesn’t explain its height.

stories.why: Both! The parents give the tree the ability to grow tall. Sun, water, soil and space decide how tall it really gets.

stories.name: A sunflower turning to the sun
stories.alt: A field of young sunflowers, all facing the same direction.
data: Young sunflowers turn to follow the sun across the sky.
Every young sunflower can do this. The ability comes from its parents.
Which way a flower points right now depends on where the sun is.
stories.stampMiss: One fact is about the parents and one is about the sun. What does that tell you?

proof.t: The ability to turn is inherited, but where it points depends on the sun.

stories.why: Both! The ability to turn is inherited. Where the flower points depends on the sun. (Grown sunflowers stop turning and face east.)

Bonde / U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain). Southern live oak with resurrection ferns, JamesDeMers, via Wikimedia Commons (CC0). verdict.win: Four cases stamped! Some traits are inherited, some come from the environment, and many are both. That’s a clue.

passiton.afterText: Which ones will her kittens get
passiton.title: Pass it on?
todo: Read each of the mother’s traits.
Guess: will it pass to her kittens, or stay with her?
Press ▶ Next generation to see what the kittens got.

why.t: A generation is one step in a family: parents are one generation, and their babies are the next.

parent.name: The mother panther
parent.alt: A trail camera photo of a Florida panther mother carrying her kitten in her mouth.

kids.name: Her three kittens
kids.alt: Three spotted Florida panther kittens with blue eyes in their den.

traits.t: A kink (a sharp bend) at the tip of her tail. She was born with it.
traits.why: Inherited traits pass down. Kinked tails were once common in Florida panther families, passed from parents to kittens.

traits.t: A scar on her nose from an old fight.
traits.why: A scar comes from something that happened to her (the environment). Her kittens are born without it.

traits.t: Round ears and a long, thick tail, like every Florida panther.
traits.short: Round ears and a long tail
traits.why: All Florida panthers inherit these from their parents. Every kitten has them too.

traits.t: She is thin because deer were hard to find this year.
traits.why: Her body changed because of not enough food (the environment). Kittens that eat well will grow to full size.

passiton.q: Why didn’t the kittens get the scar?

opts.t: The scar came from the environment, so it can’t be passed down.
The kittens are too young to have a scar yet.
opts.miss: Even when they grow up, they won’t get HER scar. Where did the scar come from?
Both parents pass down inherited traits. Where did the scar come from?

passiton.credit: Florida panther mother carrying her kitten, on a U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service trail camera, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain). Florida panther kittens in their den, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain). This panther family is part of the lesson’s story.
passiton.win: Only inherited traits pass to the next generation. Things that happen to a parent, like a scar or a hungry year, stay with that parent. That’s your last clue.

welcome.label: Welcome · one parent, two gardens
welcome.script: Hi, it’s Dr. Reyes. Last spring I collected seeds from one wild beach sunflower on the dunes. I planted some in the sunny dune garden and some in the shady courtyard. Look at the two pots in the case file. They look so different! A volunteer thinks the seeds got mixed up. Did they? Help me find out.

warmup.label: Warm-Up · find the family (Clue 1)
warmup.script: Here’s a field trick. When you match a baby to its parents, don’t look at colors first. Look at the shape: the legs, the snout, the shell. Some babies wear spots or stripes that fade later. Their body shape gives them away.

vocab.label: Word Wall
vocab.notes: Say each word. For resemble, point to a family photo.

part2.label: Part 2 · grow the twins (Clue 2)
part2.script: This is my favorite test. Two seeds, same parent. You pick the garden for each pot: sun or shade, plenty of water or a little. Then grow them. Watch which traits change, and which ones never change at all. Make sure you try one pot in the shade.

part3.label: Part 3 · stamp the case (Clue 3)
part3.script: Four Florida cases, three stamps. Inherited means from the parents. Environment means from where it lives, or something that happened to it. Both means a little of each. Read the facts, stamp it, then pick the fact that proves it.

explore.label: Part 4 · pass it on? (Clue 4)
explore.script: A panther mother just had three kittens. She has a kinked tail, a scar on her nose, and she’s thin after a hard year. Which of those will her kittens get? Make your guess for each one, then press Next generation. Don’t worry if a guess is wrong. That’s how scientists learn.

assignment.label: Assignment · crack the case
assignment.script: Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab: did my seeds get mixed up? Then answer two questions, write about a parent and its offspring, and write your CER. Your answers save as you type.

evidence.label: Use your evidence · CER
evidence.script: A classmate says babies are basically clones of their parents. Clones are exact copies. Hmm. Think about my two sunflower pots, the spotted kittens, the manatee’s scars. Are babies exact copies? Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.notes: Celebrate; tease 13.02 (how a flower makes seeds).
closing.script: Case closed! My seeds weren’t mixed up. Same parent, different gardens. The flower color and leaves came from the parent, and the sun did the rest. Next time, a new question: how did that one beach sunflower make all those seeds in the first place?

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain how animals notice and respond?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: Offspring inherit many traits from their parents, but the environment shapes other traits.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “inherit”, “parents” and “environment”. Those words carry the idea. Small words like “the” and “but” don’t.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.

tool.name: Digital calipers
tool.teaser: Measure leaves from one parent plant, grown in sun and in shade. Does the garden change the leaves?
tool.done: You measured all six leaves and found the pattern. A calipers sticker is in your Field Notebook.

why.t: A tool that measures small things very exactly. You close the jaws on the object and read the length, in millimeters (mm), on the screen.

calipers.title: Sun leaves vs. shade leaves
todo: Tap a leaf. The jaws close on it and the screen shows its length.
Measure all three leaves from each pot.
Look at the dots, then answer the question.
calipers.credit: Leaf photo: Dune sunflower leaves, Sanibel Island, James St. John, via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0). The leaf lengths are a model.

opts.t: Every leaf is exactly the same length.
opts.why: Look at the dots. Are any two leaves the same?

opts.t: The leaves vary, and the shade leaves are bigger on average.
opts.why: Yes! Leaves from one parent still vary a little (variation). And shade leaves grew bigger, to catch more of the dim light. That’s the environment at work.

opts.t: The shade plant must have a different parent.
opts.why: Both pots grew from the same parent’s seeds. What else was different between the pots?
